retro.headline: Trust Fund Commission voted unanimously to adopt nine governing documents, including the resident guide, operational manual and investment policy.
retro.summary: The chair walked through the new resident guide for applying to town trust funds, the operational manual and application forms. The two members present then adopted all nine documents in one motion. The chair also reported on the Select Board declining the warrant article, the unanswered charter question, the pending Attorney General review and a dispute with the school department over trust fund records.

what_happened.line: The Trust Fund Commission voted unanimously, by voice vote of the two members present, to adopt nine governing documents in a single motion.
The nine include the resident guide, operational manual, investment policy statement, risk mitigation policy, application forms and a resident checklist.
The chair reported the trust fund matter will not go into the special town meeting warrant; the advertisement is still to be drafted and ratified.
The commission is still waiting on pre-filing form language from the town manager before a vote and a roughly six-week Attorney General review.
The school department records dispute was not resolved; the next step is asking the Select Board to enforce the request, with discussion set for the next meeting.

why_it_matters: The adopted resident guide and forms set out how residents apply for town trust fund money, including income eligibility, savings expectations and payment directly to businesses.
With the warrant article off the special town meeting, any change to how trust funds are governed or invested waits on the Attorney General review and a later vote.
watch_next: Next meeting November 11, 2026: the school department letter, the risk management policy review and the September 10 and December 18 minutes.
The vote on the pre-filing form once the town manager supplies the language, then the Attorney General review.

retro.headline: Committee declined to change float rules for non-LHS students; FY28 capital plan led by turf/track safety fix, no votes on priorities.
retro.summary: The committee approved minutes, line item transfers, two donations and the cafeteria workers contract. It declined to pursue a policy letting non-LHS students join homecoming float, and reviewed current and FY28-FY33 capital projects, with the turf, track and retaining wall failure the top priority. It then moved to executive session on an open meeting law complaint.

what_happened.line: The School Committee ratified the cafeteria workers contract on a roll call vote that passed unanimously.
The committee voted to leave float participation as is, so non-LHS students stay under existing LHS practice; the vote result was not audible and no policy work was referred.
Members reviewed the FY28 to FY33 capital plan, with the turf, track and retaining wall failure the top priority, but took no vote on priorities.
The committee accepted line item transfers and two donations, one for Best Buddies and one of jerseys for the unified basketball team.
The facilities director was asked to add the primary school roof to the capital plan, and members want the primary boilers moved up.

why_it_matters: The capital plan sets which school building and field projects compete for a limited share of town capital money, and the turf and track work is likely to reach residents as a debt exclusion vote, which would raise tax bills.
The schools usually receive only a fraction of what they request, so items such as the roof and boilers may be delayed or left unfunded until the plan is voted.
watch_next: A later committee vote on capital priorities, which was not taken at this meeting.
The special town meeting warrant article on the turf field, mentioned in the chair's report.

retro.headline: Conservation Commission approved several wetland filings, a revised Cowry ADA trail plan advanced, and $950 Hollis Road electrical work was approved.
retro.summary: The commission heard a run of wetlands hearings, approving or issuing negative determinations on most, with conditions, and continuing others. It reviewed a revised ADA trail and parking plan at the Cowry Nature Center and heard concerns from a resident about the Unitil substation project. It also adopted the 2027 meeting schedule and approved an electrician quote for the Hollis Road house.

watch_next: Continued filings return November 4, 2026 (Cowry Nature Center, 143 Island Road, 386 Sunset Lane).
404 Page Street and the 1168 Mass Ave rear enforcement matter return November 18, 2026.

what_happened.line: The commission approved the Unitil substation notice of intent with conditions, including removal and revegetation of the former substation, 5-0.
The commission approved a negative determination with conditions for 392 Sunset Lane, and approved a septic replacement at 134 Peninsula Drive with an added planting condition, both 5-0.
After a first vote failed, the commission rescinded it and approved the 134 Crawford Street project change with a fence and boulders, 5-0.
The Cowry Nature Center ADA trail and parking plan was sent to the planning board and the notice of intent continued; the grant cannot be extended.
The commission approved the 2027 meeting schedule and an amount as heard electrician quote for the Hollis Road house, both 5-0.

why_it_matters: Approvals on the Unitil substation, septic and retaining-wall filings set the conditions that shape work near wetlands and water in Lunenburg.
The Cowry trail project is grant-funded and the grant cannot be extended, so delays in review risk the funding for an accessible trail on town conservation land.
Hollis Road house spending, a proposed caretaker position for Town Meeting and a stormwater fee question touch town property costs and possibly a future fee or tax vote.

retro.headline: Board put the track and field engineering article on the special town meeting warrant and rejected the park design article.
retro.summary: The board approved a liquor license for Kiku with a prorated fee, heard a report on selling or leasing the Brooks House, and held a joint session with the Stormwater Task Force on a utility fee versus the operating budget. It heard the superintendent on the failing track and field retaining wall, then finalized the special town meeting warrant. Track and field and the stormwater advisory were included, the accessibility/park design article failed, and the trust fund continuity bylaw failed.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to place the middle high school track and field engineering article on the special town meeting warrant.
The board voted 0-5 on the accessibility and park design article, which was moved so it could be voted down, and it did not go on the warrant.
The advisory article on stormwater funding mechanisms passed 4-1, and the trust fund continuity article failed 0-5.
The board approved the Kiku liquor license unanimously with the annual fee cut to one quarter for the rest of the calendar year.
In a joint session, the Stormwater Task Force and the board discussed a utility fee versus the operating budget; the track article was later moved to last on the warrant.

why_it_matters: Voters at the special town meeting will be asked to act on design and engineering for the track and field retaining wall, which could lead to a later construction request and tax impact.
The stormwater advisory article asks voters to weigh a dedicated utility fee against paying through the operating budget, which is funded mostly by taxes.
watch_next: October 27 Select Board meeting, where the board will make its recommendations on all special town meeting warrant articles.
The November 3 election, whose warrant the board approved, and the special town meeting warrant as finalized.

retro.headline: PACC backed a salary-line warrant request for the November warrant; its longtime chair announced resignation.
retro.summary: The committee approved minutes, heard the manager's September report, and reviewed the FY27 salaries and videographer line deficit and a warrant request. A motion to support the request as a recommendation to the town manager was made; the discussion also covered who controls the cable enterprise money and a vacation buyout charged to the salary line. The chair announced resignation effective the next day, and the committee adjourned.

what_happened.line: The Public Access Cable Committee moved to support a warrant request as a recommendation for the November warrant, pending the town manager's review; the vote was not audible.
The request combines a projected FY27 salaries shortfall with a projected videographer payroll deficit, and leaves out cost-of-living increases that are not yet known.
A vacation buyout that landed on the salaries line was backed out of the spreadsheet; whether the cable fund must later refill the salary reserve stays open.
The chair announced resignation effective the next day, and the next meeting was set for November 9 at 3 pm in the library.

why_it_matters: The cable committee's salary line is budgeted below its projected cost for FY27, so a Town Meeting warrant article may be needed to cover the gap from the cable enterprise fund.

Who controls spending from the cable enterprise fund, and whether the town can require it to replenish a reserve, were discussed but not settled, and they bear on how much of this fund is available for programming.
watch_next: The town manager's review of the warrant request ahead of the November warrant.
The committee's next meeting on November 9 at 3 pm in the library, the first after the chair's resignation.

retro.headline: Personnel Committee dropped the two-of-three voting change and began shaping a warrant article on job-description review and a class and comp study.
retro.summary: The committee discussed two possible warrant articles for town meeting: letting job descriptions with no changes within a set period skip committee review, and funding a town-wide classification and compensation study. After the town's counsel-style clarification on quorum and voting, members agreed to drop the proposal to change the voting threshold. They also planned a SharePoint-based procedures handbook and were reminded not to deliberate in a shared document outside a public meeting. No formal votes other than adjournment were taken.

what_happened.line: The Personnel Committee agreed to drop the proposal to change the voting and quorum threshold from its list of warrant items.
Members began shaping a warrant article on job-description review, including letting descriptions with no changes within a set period skip committee review.
Members said a town-wide classification and compensation study would need town meeting approval, though bids can be gathered beforehand.
An action item was set to email the HR director and town manager about the study's scope and who runs the bidding; a workshop with HR was also favored.
Members will send questions or markups to the chair individually, not comment in a shared document, to stay within open meeting law.

why_it_matters: A warrant article funding a classification and compensation study would be a town meeting vote residents are asked to take, and it bears on how town jobs are graded and paid.
The job-description change would alter how often committee review happens, which affects how openly changes to town positions get seen.
watch_next: Replies from the HR director and town manager on the study's scope and who runs the bidding.

retro.headline: Assessors voted to put two veterans-exemption articles, clauses 22I and 22J, on the November 17 town meeting warrant.
retro.summary: The board approved two sets of executive session minutes, then reviewed classification hearing preparations. The commercial and industrial valuations from Vision are a month late, and the hearing date is tight. It then voted separately to submit two Hero Act warrant articles, one tying veterans exemptions to inflation and one roughly doubling them. Town counsel may still change the wording or require staggering.

what_happened.line: The Board of Assessors voted to place two veterans-exemption articles, clauses 22I and 22J, on the town meeting warrant; the tally was not audible.
Clause 22I ties the veterans exemption increase to inflation (CPI); clause 22J would double the exemptions. The board voted on each separately.
If town counsel says both cannot be adopted in the same year, the board would propose the doubling article (22J) first; the chair will ask counsel.
The board noted the cost of the exemptions falls on the town with no state reimbursement; a member will prepare tax impact figures for the town manager.
The board prefers a Nov 24 classification hearing over Dec 1 and will press Vision for the commercial and industrial data, which is late.

why_it_matters: If town meeting adopts either article, the exemption cost is shifted onto other taxpayers' bills, because the state does not reimburse it.
The late commercial and industrial valuations could squeeze the classification hearing, which sets how the tax burden is split between homes and businesses.
watch_next: Town counsel's answer on whether 22I and 22J can both be adopted in one year, and any change to the wording.
The October 14 agenda, where pending exemption applications were deferred.
